text: Here's the scenario for this lab. A new Change Request type is rolling out, and the Change Manager has one real requirement: when a Change Request moves into the Scheduled state, the assigned Change Advisory Board group should get an email using the organization's existing Change Notification template, and if anyone on that board replies, the reply should land as a comment on the Change Request automatically — the same way incident replies already work.

Step one is writing the trigger down in plain language before touching a form: fire when a Change Request's State field changes to Scheduled. That's a record condition trigger, not an event, since there's no complex calculation involved — just a direct field transition the platform can watch for natively, and writing it down first is what you'll check the finished record against later.

Step two is identifying the recipient as its own decision, separate from the trigger. The recipient here is the assigned CAB group, not a hardcoded user and not a convenient field like Opened by. Every active member with a notification-eligible address receives a copy, and calling this out deliberately avoids picking a field that exists on the record but isn't actually who should be told.

Step three is attaching the shared Change Notification template that already exists, rather than writing a brand-new HTML body. It already carries the right placeholders for a Change Request — the number, the short description, the start and end dates for the scheduled window — each resolving against the real record when the notification fires, and any future wording fix to that template applies here automatically, too.

Step four assembles all of that into one notification record: table is Change Request, when to send is Updated, the field condition is State changes to Scheduled, who receives it is the CAB group, and the Email Template is the existing Change Notification template. Every one of those five pieces maps directly to a setting this chapter already covered — nothing here is a new mechanism.

Step five confirms the reply path actually exists, following the same pattern Lesson 18 covered for incidents: the outbound email carries a watermark identifying the specific Change Request, a reply echoes it back, inbound processing matches it, and a Record Action script appends the reply as a comment. If no Inbound Email Action exists yet for the Change Request table, that's a real gap — the outbound half can be perfect while the reply half silently does nothing.

Step six traces the whole flow end to end, on paper, before calling it finished: State set to Scheduled, trigger fires, CAB group resolved, template renders with real data, email lands, a CAB member replies, the watermark matches, and the reply becomes a comment. Every link in that chain is something this chapter already taught. Next up: UI Policies for Form Behavior, opening Chapter Five.
